variants.intertext: The number MS 3263 was given to twenty-one fragments, mostly very small, that came to light when MS 3299 (a mathematical problem text) was baked and its lower left-hand corner disintegrated in the kiln. Only one of the fragments, now 3263/9, could be rejoined to 3299 and, upon close inspection, the others turned out not to belong to that tablet at all, but to be old material joined to it in modern times with the aid of additional clay and mud. The joiner’s purpose was certainly to make MS 3299 appear complete. While some of the fragments are so small as to hold only a few wedges, others are large enough to allow the reading on them of words and parts of words. Three include names preceded by divine determinatives, @akk{{d}GIŠ} and @akk{{d}en}. These are abbreviated spellings of the heroes Gilgameš and Enkidu. Another four fragments hold phrases that can be restored as typical of the poems of Gilgameš, in particular the dream episodes that punctuate the journey to the Cedar Forest. The fragments resemble one another in script, clay and general appearance. On that account it is assumed that all twenty fragments which do not belong to MS 3299 are the extant remains of what was once a single tablet of Gilgameš. The script of what remains of this tablet is very similar to that displayed on MS 3025 (OB Schøyen₂), which reports the first two of Gilgameš’s dreams, and the two tablets were physically similar in at least one other respect (see below on Fragment 6). It seems probable that MS 3263 represents what is left of a companion piece to MS 3025, all the more so because the abbreviation den otherwise appears only in MS 3025. Because MS 3025 holds the first two dreams, it further seems likely that MS 3263 is its sequel, and began with the third dream. Its incipit is thus preserved as the catch-line of MS 3025: @i{ibrī ātamar šaluštam} “My friend, I have seen a third (dream)” (adapted from @bib{RN127@37}).

lines.translation: #tr.en: “[My friend, I have seen a third (dream).]

variants.reconstruction:
%n [... r]igmīš[a | ...]
#note: See @bib{RN127@38}: “The @i{rigmum} is presumably the screech of the @i{Anzû-}bird, and a premonition of the moment when the heroes hear Ḫuwawa’s terrible din in the distance and grow afraid (e.g. SB Gilg IV 202).”
variants.intertext: Fragment 1: MS 3263/1 is the largest fragment. It is from near the right edge, and has suffered from being cut down to shape. It contains parts of twelve lines from Gilgameš’s description of one of his dreams. This is almost certainly a variant version of the fourth dream, an account of which is also preserved on an excerpt tablet from Nippur (OB Gilg Nippur, ed. @bib{RN117@241–6}). According to that excerpt, the fourth dream was populated by a female @i{Anzû}-bird and a strange-looking man. The bird’s “radiance” (@i{šalummassa}) terrified Gilgameš but the man saved him. The present telling refers to @i{šalummatum} as a probable attribute of a feminine character (l. 3′), and to a strange-looking man (l. 6′), where the phrase matches OB Gilg Nippur. The symbolism conforms to the usual pattern of the dreams: the threatening @i{Anzû}-bird represents Ḫuwawa, whom Gilgameš shall overcome with the aid of a strange @i{eṭlum}. As Enkidu reveals in OB Gilg Nippur rev. 6′, this latter, anthropomorphic figure represents the sun god Šamaš. In the present account the arrival of the @i{eṭlum} duly heralds the rays of the sun (ll. 8′, 10′), but in language that is reminiscent of the second dream in OB Gilg Schøyen₂ (Text No. 5). The sign @i{ta} is written in such a way that the top horizontal wedge is completely obscured by the two upright wedges. This idiosyncracy sometimes also occurs on MS 3025 (Text No. 5), and is a particularly conspicuous reason for thinking that the two tablets were written by the same individual (adapted from @bib{RN127@37–38}).

lines.translation: #tr.en: [… there] was a man, strange of form,

variants.intertext: Fragment 2: MS 3263/2 is a fragment from the left edge. It contains lines that, when complete, gave an account of Enkidu’s explanation of one of Gilgameš’s dreams (adapted from @bib{RN127@38}).

Fragment 3: Another fragment from the left edge, MS 3263/3 contains traces of a dream explanation, including Enkidu’s usual reassurance that the nightmare Gilgameš has just related was, in fact, a good omen. Other such statements conclude his explanations and are followed by narrative, and that is probably also the case here (adapted from @bib{RN127@39}).

variants.reconstruction:
%n da[mqat | šunatka | ...]
#note: See @bib{RN127@39}: “Cf. OB Gilg Schøyen₂ (Text No. 5) 52: @i{dam}[@i{qā š}]@i{unātūka}; MB Gilg Boǧ₂ i 2′–3′: [@i{damqat?] šuttaka}; SB Gilg IV 28 // 109 // 155: @i{damqat šunatka}.”

lines.translation: #tr.en: Gilgameš [opened his mouth, saying to Enkidu,]

variants.intertext: Fragment 4: MS 3263/4 is the bottom left-hand corner of a tablet inscribed on obverse, edge and reverse. Enkidu puts in an appearance in l. 2′ but more than that I cannot say (adapted from @bib{RN127@40}).

Fragment 5: MS 3263/5 is a piece from the turn from obverse to bottom edge, or reverse to top edge. The presence of @i{damqat} “it is favourable” (l. 3′) suggests that the context is the end of a dream explanation (see above, Fragment 3) (adapted from @bib{RN127@40})

Fragment 6: MS 3263/6 is a fragment from the right edge that preserves the last sign of a single line, @akk{[...]-al}. The vacant spaces above and below this sign show that the scribe did not align the ends of every line with the right-hand edge of the tablet. This is also the case on OB Schøyen₂ and another reason for identifying the two tablets as companion pieces (adapted from @bib{RN127@40}).

Fragment 7: MS 3263/7 is piece from the middle inscribed with parts of four lines. If l. 2′ is correctly restored, the context is a conversation between Gilgameš and Enkidu, in which the former begins to tell the latter one of his nightmares (adapted from @bib{RN127@41}).

Fragment 11: MS 3299/11 is a piece from the left edge that contains the beginnings of two lines, the first of which comprises the word @akk{ib-r[i]} “my friend”. This word is typical of the poem of Gilgameš and clearly marks the line as the opening of a speech of Gilgameš to Enkidu or @i{vice versa}. (adapted from @bib{RN127@41}).
